newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus police clash with demonstrators.
newsitem.headline: Belarus police clash with demonstrators.

text.p: Belarus police, banging truncheons against their riot shields in a frightening staccato, clashed with demonstrators in the capital Minsk on Sunday.
Eyewitnesses said several people were slightly hurt, but there were no reports of serious injuries.
The demonstrators, who carried white and red Belarussian tricolour flags, had called their "March of Silence" to protest against a referendum called by President Alexander Lukashenko.
They say the president is seeking dictatorial powers. He says his presidency is a crusade against corruption and he has vowed to dismiss anybody who does not recognise the vote.

The march, attended by between 5,000 and 10,000 people, was the latest in a series of protests against Lukashenko's proposals, which would allow him to extend his term in office by two years without new elections.
"Long live Belarus," the marchers chanted, grumbling about Lukashenko's efforts to create a union with neighbouring Russia.

Some marchers wore cloth gags to symbolise the way the Belarussian media has covered previous protest actions of this kind. Local radio made no mention of the march, but continued its relentless drive to encourage people to turn out and vote.
The referendum officially takes place next Sunday, but polling stations are already open.
Lukashenko sent all voters a colour postcard of himself on Saturday and urged them to vote.
"Mafia clans and the owners of ill-gotten capital have united against the president you elected," Lukashenko wrote on the card, which showed him standing hand on heart in front of an adoring crowd.
"I turn to you, the honest people, to help save the country for the sake of our common future."
His supporters said people should vote before November 24, when questions drafted by parliament will also be on the ballot paper.
Some deputies have been staying in parliament around the clock because they fear the president will close the building.
Their supporters have been picketing the building and deputies have called an emergency session for Monday.
Opposition deputies have said they will start impeachment proceedings against the president, although it is not clear if this will be on the agenda at Monday's session.
Lukashenko has already shown that he will brook no opposition to his rule. On Thursday he sacked the head of the electoral commission which monitors voting in the republic of 10 million.
He has banned independent trade unions, sacked newspaper editors and closed radio stations. He threatened this week to expel two Russian television journalists.
Communists, liberals and nationalists have joined forces to oppose the president's authoritarian style, but there is no strong or united opposition and no independent media.
Some political analysts have compared the situation in Belarus to the run-up to a a bloody conflict in Russia in 1993, which President Boris Yeltsin ended by sending tanks against parliament.
